name: Port Talbot
title: Port Talbot Harbour Ship UTM | Bulk and Project Cargo Gauging
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Port Talbot harbour for bulk carriers, steel and project cargo ships and offshore vessels: holds, hatches, tanks, piping.
h1: Thickness Gauging for Ships at Port Talbot's Deep-Water Harbour
intro: Port Talbot's tidal harbour was built beside the steelworks to take the large ore and coal carriers that fed its blast furnaces. The furnaces closed in 2024, and the harbour is now between two lives: an electric arc furnace is being built at the works, and a floating offshore wind port is planned for the Celtic Sea. The ships calling in the meantime are of more varied types than the ore carriers of the past. When one needs gauging, technicians travel from India to the berth, and a docking can be arranged nearby at Swansea.

highlights.h: A deep harbour beside the works
highlights.p: The tidal harbour was designed for large bulk carriers berthing directly beside the steelworks, with no lock to pass. Ships alongside here can be gauged during cargo work, holds first as they empty, then hatch covers and ballast tanks.

highlights.h: Swansea Dry Docks across the bay
highlights.p: A ship found at Port Talbot to need steel renewal can be docked at Swansea, across the bay. Readings taken at the harbour go to the yard in advance, so plate is ordered and the work planned before the ship shifts berth.

highlights.h: Ready for the floating wind fleet
highlights.p: If the planned floating offshore wind port goes ahead, heavy-transport ships, tugs and construction vessels will use the harbour. We gauge hull, tanks and deck structure on that kind of vessel and crack-test sea-fastening points and deck fittings.

port.h: Port Talbot: a steelworks harbour in transition
p: Port Talbot stands on the eastern side of Swansea Bay, where the steelworks stretches along the shore between the town and the sea. Its tidal harbour, enclosed by breakwaters and open to the bay without a lock, was built so that large bulk carriers could bring iron ore and coal straight to the works, and for decades the harbour, owned by Associated British Ports, was the gateway for the raw materials of iron-making in the town. The Bristol Channel's big tides run through it, and the harbour is more exposed to weather from the south-west than the locked docks along the coast at Swansea and Cardiff, which a ship's master and the pilots plan around.

That role ended in 2024. Tata Steel closed the last blast furnace at the end of September, ending more than a century of primary steelmaking in Port Talbot, and construction of an electric arc furnace began in July 2025, with completion expected by the end of 2027. The works has kept its downstream mills going in the meantime, and the harbour's traffic has changed with it: the procession of large ore and coal carriers has stopped, and the ships now using the harbour are more varied. The Celtic Freeport, covering Port Talbot and Milford Haven, has had its final business case approved, and the harbour sits at the centre of plans for floating offshore wind.

In March 2026 the UK Government and ABP agreed terms for public funding, alongside ABP's own investment, to develop the harbour as a manufacturing, assembly and marshalling hub for gigawatt-scale floating wind projects from the Celtic Sea leasing round, subject to clearance by the Competition and Markets Authority. If that goes ahead, the harbour's fleet will change again: heavy-transport ships, anchor-handling tugs, construction and cable vessels and the barges that move large components. For now, gauging at Port Talbot is opportunistic, built around the ships that call and around the docking capacity a short distance away at Swansea, and each job is planned once the call is confirmed.

facilities.h: Where ships can be gauged at Port Talbot
p: Gauging at Port Talbot is done alongside the harbour's deep-water berths, during cargo operations or while a ship waits for orders. A bulk carrier discharging there can have its holds gauged as each one empties, with side shell, frames, hopper and topside tank plating, tank top and bulkheads in reach of the team; hatch covers and coamings are done when they are open, and ballast tanks once the crew can release them. The harbour sits within an industrial area, so access, vehicle movements and hot-work rules follow the port operator's site controls, which the ship's agent arranges in advance of the visit.

There is no drydock at Port Talbot. The nearest is Swansea Dry Docks, across the bay, with two graving docks that take short-sea bulk carriers, tugs and dredgers; larger ships go to a bigger yard elsewhere. Ships waiting to enter Port Talbot anchor in Swansea Bay, where a launch can put a team aboard in quiet weather, though the bay's exposure to the south-west and the strong tidal streams of the Bristol Channel mean anchorage work needs a margin in the plan. Most owners choose to gauge once the ship is alongside, where conditions are predictable and tank entry can be organised properly.
list: Deep-water harbour berths — hold, hatch-cover and ballast tank gauging on bulk carriers during discharge or loading.
Lay-by time alongside — fuller scopes on ships waiting for orders or for the next cargo.
Swansea Bay anchorage — deck, coaming and air-pipe readings by launch, in settled weather.
Swansea Dry Docks, across the bay — docking and renewal-survey gauging for ships that need steel renewed.
Future floating wind quays — hull, tank and deck-structure inspection on heavy-transport and installation vessels, as that work develops.

context.h: Port state control, the freeport and a new fleet for the Celtic Sea
p: Foreign-flagged ships calling at Port Talbot are subject to port state control by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which follows Paris MoU procedures under UK law. Bulk carriers that have spent their lives carrying ore and coal are typical inspection targets: coal cargoes leave acidic residues that eat into hold plating, frames and tank tops, and the hopper and tank-top structure of ore carriers takes heavy grab damage. An owner sending such a ship to Port Talbot with recent gauging on board, and a plan for the thin areas, gives an inspector little to question.

The floating wind plans bring vessels that sit under different rules from cargo ships. Heavy-transport ships carrying floating foundations, anchor handlers laying moorings and construction vessels are classed under their own notations and inspected by their operators to demanding project standards, and the developers' marine warranty surveyors want evidence that deck structure, sea-fastening points and towing gear are sound before a tow begins. Thickness gauging of deck plating under heavy loads and crack detection on welded fittings are part of that evidence. Until the new port is built, the work here will remain the steady, smaller business of gauging the ships that already call.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Port Talbot
jobs.p: Work at Port Talbot depends on what is calling, and we plan each job with the superintendent and the ship's agent once the berth and stay are confirmed. Most jobs today are in-service gauging on cargo ships alongside, often as preparation for a survey or a docking elsewhere. As the floating wind project moves forward, we expect offshore vessels to add a second strand of work. Where the readings point to steel renewal, the obvious next step is a docking across the bay at Swansea, and we pass the figures to the yard in a form it can plan from. These are the jobs we expect to see most often.
list: Hold, hopper and tank-top gauging on a bulk carrier during discharge, focused on cargo-related wastage and grab damage.
Pre-docking steel estimate on a ship due to dock at Swansea, taken at Port Talbot before it shifts across the bay.
Hatch cover and coaming gauging on a project or steel cargo ship alongside the harbour berths.
Owner's condition gauging on a ship waiting for orders, using the time alongside for ballast tanks and deck structure.
Deck plating gauging and MPI of sea-fastening points on a heavy-transport or offshore vessel, as floating wind activity grows.

logistics: Cardiff Airport is the closest international airport, with Bristol Airport as an alternative; most teams fly into Heathrow and take the train from London Paddington to Port Talbot Parkway. The harbour is a controlled port inside an industrial area, so the ship's agent arranges passes and any site induction before the visit. Technicians are mobilised from India on UK visas, and because calls at Port Talbot are irregular, we plan with a margin around the expected arrival and keep visas current for owners who use the harbour often.

faqs.q: Is Port Talbot still a working harbour after the blast furnaces closed?
faqs.a: Yes. The harbour remains open under Associated British Ports, though its traffic has changed now that iron ore and coal no longer arrive for the furnaces. Ships still call, and the harbour is the focus of the Celtic Freeport and of plans for a floating offshore wind port. We gauge whatever is calling, on the owner's or manager's instructions, during its time alongside.

faqs.q: Where would a ship calling at Port Talbot go for a drydock?
faqs.a: The nearest drydocks are at Swansea Dry Docks, across the bay, which take short-sea bulk carriers, tugs and dredgers. Larger ships dock at a bigger yard elsewhere in the UK or abroad. Either way, gauging at Port Talbot before the ship leaves gives the yard a list of plate and pipe to renew, so the docking can be planned and material ordered in advance.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged during discharge at Port Talbot?
faqs.a: Yes, hold by hold, once each is empty and safe to enter. The team gauges side shell, frames, hopper and topside tank plating and the tank top, paying close attention to areas damaged by grabs or thinned by corrosive cargo residues. Hatch covers and coamings are done while open, and ballast tanks after the crew issue entry permits.

faqs.q: Will you inspect vessels for the Celtic Sea floating wind projects?
faqs.a: Yes, as that work begins. Heavy-transport ships, anchor handlers and construction vessels need deck plating, tank structure and sea-fastening points checked before demanding operations, and operators often want readings before a project mobilisation. We gauge hull, tanks and deck structure and crack-test welded fittings by magnetic particle or dye penetrant, planned with the operator around the vessel's project schedule.

faqs.q: Does weather in Swansea Bay affect gauging at Port Talbot?
faqs.a: Alongside, very little: the harbour's breakwaters give working shelter, and the inspection carries on in most conditions. At anchor in the bay it matters more, because south-westerly winds and strong tidal streams can make launch transfers unsafe. We plan anchorage work only for short, deck-level scopes, keep a weather margin, and move the work alongside if conditions turn.
